newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesians vote against backdrop of violence.
newsitem.headline: Indonesians vote against backdrop of violence.

text.p: Indonesians vote on Thursday in elections described by the government as "a festival of democracy" but marred by the worst political violence in 30 years and several bomb threats in the capital.
The ruling Golkar is assured of a comfortable victory, but analysts are watching the reaction to the results of the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP).

The only other party legally permitted to run, the Christian-Nationalist Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI), has been badly hit by a leadership battle and was virtually sidelined during the 27-day campaign that ended last Friday.
Analysts are also watching for the size of Golput, or "White Party", the term used for people who spoil their ballots or abstain as a form of protest.

The PPP posed a strong challenge to Golkar during a campaign hit by violence, mainly between partisans of the two groups, and political analysts said further trouble might erupt if the PPP felt it had been cheated.

The Japanese embassy in the central business area was evacuated on Wednesday morning after an unidentified man said there was a bomb in the building. The police bomb squad found no sign of explosives.

Official sources said there had been a couple of other isolated bomb warnings and also rumours of threats in different parts of Jakarta on Tuesday, and news reports said the army had arrested four men they believed were planning to set off an explosion in a North Jakarta shopping mall.
Despite the threats and tension in some areas of the city of more than 10 million, businesses were open and traffic was normal.

Nearly 125 million people in the world's fourth most populous nation are eligible to vote for 425 elected seats in the House of Representatives. The other 75 seats are filled by the military which does not vote.

Polls open from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. (0100-0700 GMT) with major results likely known within 24 hours. Final results will trickle in over a week from the archipelago of more than 17,500 islands stretching 5,000 km (3,000 miles) along the equator.
The election campaign hit a violent peak on its final day last Friday, with riots and a shopping mall fire in the capital of South Kalimantan province on Borneo island killing more than 120 people.

Political analysts blamed the violence on political rivalry, youthful exuberance and dissatisfaction and frustration with the government and system during an outpouring of political passion allowed only once every five years.
"I haven't seen before such intense anger, jealousy and frustration," political commentator Mochtar Buchori told Reuters.
The country has been quiet during the subsequent five-day cooling off period.
Golkar, in power for most of President Suharto's 30-year rule, won 68 percent of the vote at the last elections in 1992 and is seeking just over 70 percent this time round.
The PPP hopes for a strong showing in its traditional areas of support in Central and Western Java, including Jakarta itself.
A senior Asian diplomat said feelings appeared fairly relaxed, but there was concern over what might happen if the PPP share of the vote did not live up to expectations.
"The business community in Jakarta expects that if the results are not what would have been expected by the PPP, they might find some way of protesting the result," he said.
Markets were steady on Wednesday but trading was slow.
Other diplomats said businessmen were wary of the immediate post-election period for fear of trouble.
